title: Part 830: NTSB Accident Reporting
description: Master NTSB accident and incident notification and reporting requirements from 49 CFR Part 830

questions.question: What is the definition of an aircraft accident?
options: An occurrence resulting in death, serious injury, or substantial damage between boarding and deplaning
Any incident requiring an emergency landing
Any event that grounds an aircraft
questions.explanation: Per 49 CFR 830.2, an aircraft accident is an occurrence associated with aircraft operation from boarding to deplaning that results in death, serious injury, or substantial damage.

questions.question: What is considered 'substantial damage' to an aircraft?
options: Damage that adversely affects structural strength, performance, or flight characteristics requiring major repair or replacement
questions.explanation: Per 49 CFR 830.2, substantial damage adversely affects structural strength, performance, or flight characteristics and requires major repair or component replacement.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT considered substantial damage?
options: Damaged landing gear requiring major repair
questions.explanation: Per 49 CFR 830.2, damage to fairings, cowlings, small dents, or holes is specifically excluded from the definition of substantial damage.

questions.question: What is a 'serious injury' under Part 830?
options: Hospitalization for more than 48 hours within 7 days, fractures (except simple), severe hemorrhage, nerve/muscle/tendon damage, internal organ injury, or burns
Any injury preventing return to work
questions.explanation: Per 49 CFR 830.2, serious injury includes hospitalization >48 hours within 7 days, bone fractures (except simple nose/finger/toe), severe hemorrhage, nerve/muscle/tendon damage, internal organ injury, or 2nd/3rd degree burns >5% of body.

questions.question: When must the NTSB be notified of an aircraft accident?
questions.explanation: Per 49 CFR 830.5, the operator must notify the NTSB immediately of any aircraft accident.

questions.question: Who is responsible for notifying the NTSB of an accident?
questions.explanation: Per 49 CFR 830.5, the operator of an aircraft is responsible for immediately notifying the NTSB.

questions.question: Which incident requires immediate notification to the NTSB?
options: A hard landing with no damage
Flight control system malfunction or failure
questions.explanation: Per 49 CFR 830.5, flight control system malfunction or failure is one of the incidents requiring immediate NTSB notification.

questions.question: An in-flight fire requires:
options: No notification unless there is damage
Notification only if passengers are aboard
questions.explanation: Per 49 CFR 830.5, in-flight fire is an incident requiring immediate NTSB notification.

questions.question: When is a written report required to be filed with the NTSB?
options: Within 10 days of an accident or when requested for an incident
Only when requested by the FAA
questions.explanation: Per 49 CFR 830.15, a written report (NTSB Form 6120.1) must be filed within 10 days of an accident, or when requested for an incident.

questions.question: An aircraft overdue and believed to be involved in an accident requires:
questions.explanation: Per 49 CFR 830.5, an aircraft that is overdue and believed to have been involved in an accident requires immediate NTSB notification.

questions.question: What information must be provided in the immediate notification to NTSB?
options: Only the location of the accident
Type of aircraft, name of operator, names of crew, date/time, location, nature of accident, injuries, and damage
Only the pilot's name and certificate number
questions.explanation: Per 49 CFR 830.6, immediate notification must include aircraft type, operator, crew names, date/time, location, last departure point, nature of accident, injuries, and damage extent.

questions.question: A mid-air collision requires:
options: Notification only if there is injury or damage
No notification if both aircraft land safely
questions.explanation: Per 49 CFR 830.5, collision between aircraft in flight requires immediate NTSB notification, regardless of damage or injury.

questions.question: May aircraft wreckage be moved before the NTSB arrives?
options: Only to protect the wreckage, prevent further damage, or protect public
questions.explanation: Per 49 CFR 830.10, wreckage may only be moved to protect it from further damage, remove persons, or protect the public from injury.

questions.question: If wreckage must be moved before NTSB investigation, what must be done?
options: Sketches, photographs, and notes must be made of original positions
questions.explanation: Per 49 CFR 830.10, if wreckage must be moved, sketches, descriptive notes, and photographs must be made of the original positions and condition.

questions.question: Damage limited to the engine does NOT constitute substantial damage if:
options: The damage is limited to the engine, bent cowling, dented skin, small holes, or damage to rotor/prop blades, landing gear, etc.
questions.explanation: Per 49 CFR 830.2, engine damage, bent fairings/cowling, dented skin, small holes, and damage to landing gear, flaps, rotor/prop blades are specifically excluded from substantial damage.

questions.question: An in-flight engine failure requiring a forced landing is:
options: An accident if there is substantial damage
Always an incident requiring immediate notification
Only reportable if there are injuries
questions.explanation: Engine failure alone is not an immediately reportable incident. It becomes an accident only if it results in death, serious injury, or substantial damage.

questions.question: Release of all or a portion of a propeller blade from an aircraft requires:
questions.explanation: Per 49 CFR 830.5, release of all or a portion of a propeller blade from an aircraft is an incident requiring immediate NTSB notification.

questions.question: Failure of any internal turbine engine component resulting in escape of debris requires:
options: Notification only if damage to aircraft
questions.explanation: Per 49 CFR 830.5, turbine engine failure with debris escape through the engine exhaust case or causing structural damage requires immediate NTSB notification.

questions.question: An aircraft evacuation using emergency egress systems requires:
questions.explanation: Per 49 CFR 830.5, an aircraft evacuation using emergency egress systems is an incident requiring immediate NTSB notification.

questions.question: How can the NTSB be notified of an accident?
questions.explanation: Per 49 CFR 830.5, notification must be made by the most expeditious means available. This typically means telephone to the nearest NTSB office.
